title: Transmission Control Protocol

hero.subtitle: Reliable, ordered, and connection-oriented byte stream delivery over IP

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) is a connection-oriented, reliable transport protocol that provides a full-duplex byte stream service between applications. It is the workhorse behind most long-lived Internet connections.

TCP guarantees that data arrives complete, in order, and without corruption. If packets are lost, TCP automatically retransmits them. If they arrive out of order, TCP resequences them.
sections.plainLanguage: The Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) gives applications a reliable, two-way stream of bytes. It guarantees that data arrives complete, in order and uncorrupted. It does this by retransmitting lost packets and reordering packets that arrive out of sequence.

sections.title: Philosophy
sections.content:
TCP implements the end-to-end principle: reliability is provided at the endpoints, not in the network itself. The network (IP) provides best-effort delivery, and TCP adds reliability on top.

Reliable Delivery
Every byte sent is acknowledged. Lost data is retransmitted. Duplicate data is discarded. Applications see a clean, reliable byte stream.
Flow Control
The receiver advertises a window size indicating how much data it can buffer. The sender never overwhelms the receiver.
Congestion Control (added later)
RFC 793 does not define congestion control; later specifications such as RFC 5681 add it. TCP then adapts its sending rate to avoid overwhelming the network. Algorithms like slow start and congestion avoidance dynamically adjust throughput.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP provides reliability at the two endpoints, not inside the network, which only offers best-effort delivery through IP. Every byte is acknowledged, lost data is resent and duplicates are discarded. The receiver advertises a window, which limits how much the sender may send. Congestion control was added by later RFCs.

sections.title: Concepts
sections.content:
TCP introduces several fundamental concepts:

ConnectionA pair of endpoints (IP:port) forming a reliable communication channel
SegmentA unit of data sent by TCP, containing a header and optional payload
Sequence NumberIdentifies each byte in the stream; used for ordering and duplicate detection
AcknowledgmentConfirms receipt of data up to a given sequence number
WindowThe amount of data the receiver is willing to accept
SocketAn IP address + port number pair identifying one end of a connection
sections.plainLanguage: A connection joins two endpoints, each an IP address and port pair called a socket. Data travels in segments. Each byte has a sequence number used for ordering and detecting duplicates. An acknowledgment confirms data received up to a given number, and the window is the amount the receiver will accept.

sections.title: Header Format
sections.content:
The TCP header is 20 bytes long when no options are present, and always a whole number of 32-bit words (RFC 793 Figure 3). Options, if any, follow the Urgent Pointer and are padded so that the header ends on a 32-bit boundary; the data follows.

In RFC 793 the six control bits are URG, ACK, PSH, RST, SYN and FIN, and the 6 bits before them are reserved. The ECE and CWR flags shown in many modern diagrams were added later (RFC 3168) by taking two of those reserved bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The TCP header is 20 bytes without options and always a whole number of 32-bit words. It carries ports, sequence and acknowledgment numbers, a window, a checksum and control bits (URG, ACK, PSH, RST, SYN and FIN). Options follow the header and are padded to a 32-bit boundary.

sections.title: Connection Management
sections.content:
TCP uses a three-way handshake to establish connections and a four-way handshake to close them:

Opening: Three-Way Handshake
1. Client sends SYN with initial sequence number x. 2. Server responds with SYN-ACK, its own sequence number y, and acknowledgment x+1. 3. Client sends ACK with acknowledgment y+1. Connection is now established.
Closing: Four-Way Handshake
1. Initiator sends FIN. 2. Receiver acknowledges with ACK. 3. Receiver sends its own FIN. 4. Initiator acknowledges with ACK. Both directions are now closed.
Reset
The RST flag immediately aborts a connection without the graceful close procedure. Used when an error condition is detected or a connection is refused.

The SYN and FIN flags each consume one sequence number, even though they carry no data. This ensures they are reliably delivered through the same acknowledgment mechanism as data.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP opens a connection with a three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, then ACK, with each side giving its starting sequence number. It closes with a four-way handshake of FIN and ACK in each direction. A RST flag aborts a connection immediately after an error or refusal.

sections.title: Data Transfer
sections.content:
Once a connection is established, TCP provides reliable bidirectional data transfer using sequence numbers and acknowledgments.

Sliding Window
TCP uses a sliding window mechanism for flow control. The sender can transmit up to the window size without waiting for acknowledgments, enabling efficient use of the network.
Retransmission
If an acknowledgment is not received within a timeout period (RTO), TCP retransmits the unacknowledged data. The RTO is dynamically computed based on measured round-trip times.
Cumulative ACKs
Each ACK confirms receipt of all bytes up to the acknowledgment number. This allows a single ACK to cover multiple segments received.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP uses a sliding window, so the sender can transmit up to the window size without waiting for acknowledgments. Each ACK is cumulative, covering all bytes up to its number. If no ACK arrives before a timeout, based on measured round-trip times, TCP retransmits the data.

sections.title: Reliability
sections.content:
TCP achieves reliable delivery through several cooperating mechanisms:

Mechanism
Purpose
Checksums
Detect corrupted segments
Sequence Numbers
Order segments and detect duplicates
Acknowledgments
Confirm data receipt
Retransmission Timer
Detect and recover from loss
Flow Control (Window)
Prevent receiver buffer overflow
Congestion Control (added later)
Prevent network overload
sections.plainLanguage: TCP combines several mechanisms for reliability. Checksums detect corrupted segments, sequence numbers keep order and spot duplicates, and acknowledgments confirm receipt. A retransmission timer recovers from loss, and the window prevents receiver buffer overflow. Congestion control came later.

subtitle: Reliable, ordered, connection-oriented byte-stream delivery over IP
summary: TCP gives two programs on different hosts a reliable, ordered, two-way stream of bytes on top of unreliable IP datagrams. It numbers every byte, acknowledges what arrives, retransmits what does not, and lets the receiver throttle the sender with a window. Connections are opened with a three-way handshake and closed with FIN segments.

plainLanguage.summary: TCP gives two programs on different hosts a reliable, ordered, two-way stream of bytes over unreliable IP datagrams. It numbers every byte, acknowledges what arrives and retransmits what does not. The receiver can throttle the sender with a window. Connections open with a three-way handshake and close with FIN segments.

tldr.problem: IP delivers packets on a best-effort basis: they can be lost, duplicated, damaged or reordered, but applications want a dependable stream.
tldr.mechanism: TCP numbers every byte with a sequence number, the receiver acknowledges the next byte it expects, the sender retransmits on timeout, and a window field limits how much may be in flight.
tldr.outcome: Applications see a full-duplex, in-order byte stream, and TCP became the transport under most of the Internet's long-lived traffic.

facts.label: Control bits
facts.value: URG, ACK, PSH, RST, SYN, FIN

today: TCP is still the transport under HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, SMTP, SSH and TLS-protected traffic, though RFC 793 itself has been replaced by RFC 9293, which folds in decades of fixes. Congestion control, window scaling, selective acknowledgments and explicit congestion notification were all added later. HTTP/3 now runs over QUIC on UDP instead.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Sequence number of the first data octet in this segment, except when SYN is present; then it is the initial sequence number (ISN) and the first data octet is ISN+1.

fields.name: Acknowledgment Number
fields.desc: If ACK is set, the next sequence number the sender of the segment expects to receive. Always sent once a connection is established.

fields.name: Data Offset
fields.desc: Number of 32-bit words in the TCP header; it tells where the data begins.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Reserved for future use. Must be zero.

fields.name: Control Bits
fields.desc: From left to right: URG (urgent pointer significant), ACK (acknowledgment field significant), PSH (push function), RST (reset the connection), SYN (synchronize sequence numbers), FIN (no more data from sender).

fields.name: Window
fields.desc: The number of data octets, beginning with the one in the acknowledgment field, that the sender of this segment is willing to accept.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of all 16-bit words in the header and text, plus a pseudo header taken from the IP header.

fields.name: Urgent Pointer
fields.desc: Offset from the sequence number of the octet that follows the urgent data. Only significant when URG is set.
